whatItIs.text: Rice-grain-shaped pasta of durum wheat — the Italians call it risoni, 'large grains of rice', because in Italy orzo means barley.

historyNote.text: Every Mediterranean kitchen named the shape independently: Greek kritharáki ('little barley'), Turkish arpa şehriye, Egyptian lisān al-ʿaṣfūr ('bird's tongue'); Israel developed its own rice-substitute version, ptitim, in the 1950s.

howToChoose.text: Choose bronze-cut orzo if you can find it — rough surfaces hold sauce; check freshness dates since its small size goes stale invisibly.

storage.text: Keep in a sealed box in a dry cupboard; cooked, it needs the fridge.

useItUp.text: Leftover orzo fries like rice, bakes into casseroles (giouvetsi-style), or thickens soup; toast it dry in butter first for a nutty pilaf.
